hints: Look at each distinct part of P separately, the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ ends, the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ link, the $\text{Cl}$ atom, and the six membered ring, and recall the family name for each.
Remember that a halogen attached to a benzene ring is named as chloro plus benzene or arene, and a $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group has its own family name distinct from amine.
walkthrough:
Spot the triple bonded carbon nitrogen groups**
On the right hand side you see two $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ groups. That $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ unit is the nitrile group. It behaves quite differently from an amine, so keep the name nitrile.

Spot the carbon carbon double bond**
In the middle of P there is $\text{H-C}=\text{C(CN)}_{2}$. A $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond between two carbons defines the alkene family. That gives the second name for the first mark.

Name the ring and its substituent**
On the left you have a benzene ring with a $\text{Cl}$ atom directly attached. Think of this as two features together, a chloro substituent and a benzene or arene ring system. That pairing gives the second mark.

Final answer: nitrile ($\text{CN}$) and alkene ($\text{C}=\text{C}$)
chloro ($\text{Cl}$) and benzene / arene ring

hints: Decide which bond in P can open to join to neighbours, recall that polymerisation of this type uses only the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond while all other groups stay unchanged.
Recall how a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ becomes a $\text{-C-C-}$ backbone in the polymer, and think about whether any small molecule is lost when only a double bond opens.
walkthrough:
See what polymerises**
Only the alkene $\text{C}=\text{C}$ takes part. The 2-chlorophenyl ring and the two $\text{CN}$ groups are spectators, they just ride along on the new chain. So picture the double bond opening to a single bond.

Build the saturated backbone**
Each monomer $\text{(2-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{)CH}=\text{C(CN)}_{2}$ becomes $\text{-CH(2-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{)-C(CN)}_{2}\text{-}$ in the polymer. Join two of these units head to tail and add short continuation bonds through the brackets at both ends to show the chain continues.

Name the process**
Because the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ simply adds across itself with no other product lost, no $\text{HCl}$ or water expelled, this is addition polymerisation, not condensation.

Final answer: Polymer section (two repeat units joined): $\text{-[CH(2-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{)-C(CN)}_{2}\text{]- [CH(2-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{)-C(CN)}_{2}\text{]-}$ with continuation bonds at each end.
type of polymerisation: addition (polymerisation)

hints: Start by listing for P which site each reagent attacks first, the $\text{C}=\text{C}$, the $\text{CN}$ groups, or the benzene ring.
For $\text{Br}_{2}\text{(aq)}$, recall what happens when $\text{Br-Br}$ adds across an isolated $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and whether the ring or $\text{CN}$ reacts under mild conditions.
For hot concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$, recall that a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ is cleaved completely, with each alkene carbon becoming a carbonyl or carboxyl carbon.
Think about which fragment from that cleavage still carries the 2-chlorophenyl group and what it becomes on strong oxidation.
For hot aqueous $\text{HCl}$, recall the hydrolysis pattern $\text{RCN} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCOOH} + \text{NH}_{3}$ under acidic conditions.
Count how many $\text{CN}$ groups are hydrolysed in P and decide whether the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ survives hot dilute acid.
For $\text{H}_{2}$ with Pt, recall the three reducible units here, alkene to alkane, nitrile to primary amine, and benzene ring under forcing conditions.
Match each transformation to its reaction type label, addition, oxidation, hydrolysis, and reduction or hydrogenation.
walkthrough:
Addition of bromine across the double bond**
Picture $\text{Br}_{2}$ approaching the electron rich $\text{C}=\text{C}$. The pi bond breaks and one $\text{Br}$ adds to each carbon. You get $(2\text{-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{CH(Br)-C(Br)(CN)}_{2}$. The benzene ring and the $\text{CN}$ groups do not react with bromine water under these conditions. This is electrophilic addition.

Strong oxidation cleaves the alkene**
Hot concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ is a powerful oxidiser that cuts the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ right in half. Think of $$\text{(2-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{)CH}=\text{C(CN)}_{2} \rightarrow \text{(2-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{)CH} + \text{C(CN)}_{2}$$ followed by oxidation to the highest oxidation level.

Identify the two oxidation fragments**
The left carbon attached to the ring becomes 2-chlorobenzoic acid, $2\text{-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COOH}$. The right carbon $\text{C(CN)}_{2}$ becomes $\text{O=C(CN)}_{2}$, which under vigorous conditions can be further oxidised to ethanedioic acid, $\text{HOOC-COOH}$. This is oxidation.

Acid hydrolysis targets the nitriles**
Hot aqueous $\text{HCl}$ hydrolyses nitriles: $$\text{RCN} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCOOH} + \text{NH}_{3}$$ which in acid appears as $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$. Here both $\text{CN}$ groups on the same carbon hydrolyse, so $\text{C(CN)}_{2}$ becomes $\text{C(COOH)}_{2}$. The $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and the chloroarene survive, giving $(2\text{-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{CH}=\text{C(COOH)}_{2}$. This is hydrolysis.

Catalytic hydrogenation reduces everything unsaturated**
With excess $\text{H}_{2}$ over Pt, three reductions happen together. The alkene $\text{CH}=\text{C}$ gains $\text{H}_{2}$ to give $\text{CH}_{2}\text{-CH}$. Each nitrile gains $2\text{H}_{2}$: $$\text{RCN} + 2\text{H}_{2} \rightarrow \text{RCH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$$ so you get two $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ groups. With excess and Pt, the benzene ring is also hydrogenated to a cyclohexane ring. This is reduction, also called hydrogenation.

Final answer: excess $\text{Br}_{2}\text{(aq)}$: $(2\text{-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{CH(Br)-C(Br)(CN)}_{2}$; (electrophilic) addition
excess hot conc. acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}\text{(aq)}$: $2\text{-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{COOH}$ + $\text{O=C(CN)}_{2}$ or $\text{HOOC-COOH}$; oxidation
excess hot $\text{HCl(aq)}$: $(2\text{-ClC}_{6}\text{H}_{4})\text{CH=C(COOH)}_{2}$ + $2\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$; hydrolysis (acid hydrolysis)
excess $\text{H}_{2}$/Pt: $(2\text{-chlorocyclohexyl)CH}_{2}\text{-CH(CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2})_{2}$ i.e. alkene reduced to single bond, both $\text{CN}$ to $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, benzene reduced to cyclohexane; reduction / hydrogenation
